title: Kathmandu valley heritage on a saver budget
start: Kathmandu, Tribhuvan International Airport or Thamel
price_note: Per person, twin sharing: 4 nights in a hostel private room and simple guesthouses, local buses and shared taxis, SAARC-rate entry fees, a half-day licensed guide in Patan; flights or buses to Kathmandu and most meals extra.
transport: Local buses, microbuses and shared taxis
meta_description: Kathmandu valley in 4 nights on a saver budget: Durbar Square, Swayambhunath, Patan, Bhaktapur and a Nagarkot sunrise by local bus, from ₹12,500.
summary: Four nights across the three old royal cities of the Kathmandu valley and a ridge-top sunrise, on local buses and in simple rooms. Two nights in Thamel for Kathmandu Durbar Square, Swayambhunath, Boudhanath and Patan, one in Bhaktapur's old town and one at Nagarkot facing the Himalaya.
intro: The Kathmandu valley has seven UNESCO-listed monument zones within about 20 km of each other, and almost all of them are reachable by a local bus that costs less than a cup of coffee in Thamel. That makes it one of the best-value heritage trips in South Asia for Indian travellers, who also pay the lower SAARC entry rates on showing a passport or voter ID.

We keep this trip honest and simple. You sleep in a private room at Zostel Kathmandu, then in a family guesthouse inside Bhaktapur's car-free old town and a basic lodge on the Nagarkot ridge. Buses are crowded and rooms are plain, sometimes with shared bathrooms in Bhaktapur. In return you see the valley at its own pace, eat in Newar kitchens and spend less than ₹3,500 a day.
highlights: Kathmandu Durbar Square and the Kumari Ghar with a SAARC-rate ticket
Sunset over the valley from the Swayambhunath stupa
Patan's Krishna Mandir and the Patan Museum with a licensed guide
A night inside Bhaktapur's old town after the day visitors leave
Sunrise over the Langtang and Ganesh Himal ranges from Nagarkot

days.title: Arrive Kathmandu, Thamel and Asan
days.text: Arrive at Tribhuvan airport or the Sorhakhutte bus park. A pre-paid taxi to Thamel costs about NPR 700–1,000; a Pathao or InDrive ride is often cheaper. Check in at Zostel, change money at the fixed rate of 1 INR to 1.6 NPR, and buy a local SIM with your passport. In the late afternoon walk south from Thamel through Asan and Indra Chowk, the old trading lanes, to Kathmandu Durbar Square. Dinner: buff or veg momos at a local momo house for about ₹150.

days.title: Durbar Square, Swayambhunath, Boudhanath
days.text: Start at Kathmandu Durbar Square at opening time, before the tour groups, and see the Kumari Ghar courtyard and the Hanuman Dhoka palace. Walk west over the Vishnumati to climb the 365 steps of Swayambhunath. After lunch take a microbus or shared taxi east to Boudhanath, one of the largest stupas in the world, and walk the kora clockwise with the Tibetan families at dusk. Return to Thamel by microbus or taxi.

days.title: Patan by bus, on to Bhaktapur
days.text: Take a microbus from Ratna Park to Patan Dhoka, about 40 minutes. A licensed guide shows you Patan Durbar Square for half a day: the stone Krishna Mandir, the Golden Temple a few lanes north and the Patan Museum, whose ticket is included in the square's entry. After a Newari set lunch, ride back to Ratna Park and on to Bhaktapur by local bus. Check into a guesthouse inside the old town and walk Taumadhi Square at dusk.

days.title: Bhaktapur morning, bus to Nagarkot
days.overnight: Simple lodge on the Nagarkot ridge
days.text: Early morning in Bhaktapur is for the potters' square, where clay is shaped and dried in the sun, and for juju dhau, the town's thick sweet curd, from a shop near Nyatapola. Walk to Dattatreya Square and the peacock window. After lunch, catch a local bus from the Bhaktapur bus park to Nagarkot. Check into a ridge lodge, walk to a viewpoint for sunset and have dal bhat early.

days.title: Nagarkot sunrise, back to Kathmandu
days.text: Be at the viewpoint before dawn: in clear months the line from Langtang to the Ganesh Himal and, far east, a glimpse of the Everest group catches the first light. After breakfast take a local bus back to Bhaktapur and change for Kathmandu, or walk 3–4 hours down the trail to Changu Narayan, the valley's oldest temple, and take a bus from there. Reach Thamel by early afternoon.

includes: 2 nights at Zostel Kathmandu in a private room, twin sharing
1 night in a simple Bhaktapur guesthouse and 1 night in a basic Nagarkot lodge
All local bus, microbus and shared-taxi fares on the route
SAARC-rate entry to Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur Durbar Squares and Swayambhunath
excludes: Flights or buses to and from Kathmandu
Boudhanath and Changu Narayan entry fees
good_to_know: Indian citizens need a passport or Election Commission voter ID to enter Nepal and to claim SAARC entry rates; Aadhaar is not accepted for adults.
Bhaktapur guesthouses are old Newar houses with steep wooden stairs and low doorways; some rooms share a bathroom.
Winter smog can hide the mountains at Nagarkot after mid-morning; October to early December gives the clearest views.
Local buses do not have luggage holds; travel with one backpack and leave extra bags at Zostel.
Nagarkot is at about 2,175 m: cold at night from November to February, but not high enough for altitude problems.

faqs.q: How much does a 4-night Kathmandu valley trip cost on a budget?
faqs.a: This trip starts at ₹12,500 per person, twin sharing, covering rooms, breakfasts, local transport, SAARC-rate entry fees and a Patan guide. Add ₹600–900 a day for other meals. Flights from Delhi to Kathmandu or a bus via the Sunauli border are extra. Travellers who share dorm beds can cut the room cost further.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a passport to visit Kathmandu?
faqs.a: No visa is needed, but adults must carry either a valid Indian passport or an Election Commission voter ID card. Aadhaar and PAN cards are not accepted for entry. The same ID gets you the lower SAARC rates at Durbar Squares. Rules can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it safe to use local buses in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Yes, local buses and microbuses are safe and used by everyone, but they are crowded at rush hour and pickpocketing happens. Keep your phone and wallet in a front pocket. Conductors call out destinations; ask fellow passengers if unsure. Women often sit in the front seats, some of which are reserved for women.

faqs.q: Can I see all three Durbar Squares in one day?
faqs.a: You can, but it is a rush and you would see little. We spread them over three days so each gets a morning or afternoon at a sensible pace. If you are short of time, prioritise Bhaktapur, which is the best preserved, then Patan.

faqs.q: What is the best month for Kathmandu sightseeing?
faqs.a: October to December is clearest, with mild days and mountain views from Nagarkot. February and March are also good. Avoid June to August if you want views; the monsoon brings heavy afternoon rain, though the temples are quiet and festivals like Gai Jatra fall in August.

faqs.q: Is Zostel Kathmandu good for couples?
faqs.a: Yes, Zostel Kathmandu offers private rooms as well as dorms, and its Thamel location puts Durbar Square and Asan within walking distance. It is a social hostel, so expect common areas with other travellers. Couples who want more quiet can upgrade to a guesthouse in the Thamel side lanes.

faqs.q: What should I eat in the Kathmandu valley?
faqs.a: Try momos in Kathmandu, a Newari samay baji set of beaten rice, spiced meat, egg and soybeans in Patan or Bhaktapur, and juju dhau, the King of Curd, in Bhaktapur. Dal bhat is the everyday meal with refills included. Vegetarians eat well in all three cities.

faqs.q: Can I add Chitwan or Pokhara to this trip?
faqs.a: Yes. Tourist buses leave Kathmandu for Pokhara and Chitwan each morning for about ₹500–1,600 a seat. Pokhara adds the lake and Annapurna views; see our Pokhara and Poon Hill saver trip. We can quote the combined journey on request.

faqs.q: Do I need cash in Nepal?
faqs.a: Yes. Many guesthouses, buses and small eateries take cash only. ATMs in Thamel and Bhaktapur work with Indian cards, but fees apply. Indian ₹100 notes are widely accepted; ₹500 and higher notes have had restrictions in Nepal for years, so check current status before you travel.
